question_en: An annual-pay, 4% coupon, 10-year bond has a yield to maturity of 5.2%. If the price of this bond is unchanged two years later, its yield to maturity at that time is:
explanation_en: This bond is priced at a discount to par value because its 4% coupon is less than its 5.2% yield to maturity. As the bond gets closer to maturity, the discount will amortize toward par value, which means its price will increase if its yield remains unchanged. For its price to remain unchanged, its yield would have to increase. Price with 10 years to maturity: N = 10; I/Y = 5.2; PMT = 40; FV = 1,000; CPT PV = –908.23 Yield with 8 years to maturity: N = 8; PMT = 40; FV = 1,000; PV = –908.23; CPT I/Y = 5.446%

question_en: Other things equal, for option-free bonds:
option_a: a bond’s value is more sensitive to yield increases than to yield decreases.
option_b: the value of a long-term bond is more sensitive to interest rate changes than the value of a short-term bond.
option_c: the value of a low-coupon bond is less sensitive to interest rate changes than the value of a high-coupon bond.
explanation_en: Long-term, low-coupon bonds are more sensitive than short-term and high-coupon bonds. Prices are more sensitive to rate decreases than to rate increases (duration rises as yields fall).

question_en: A year ago a company issued a bond with a face value of $1,000 with an 8% coupon. Now the prevailing market yield is 10%. What happens to the bond? The bond:
option_a: is traded at a market price higher than $1,000.
option_b: is traded at a market price of less than $1,000.
option_c: price is not affected by the change in market yield, and will continue to trade at $1,000.
explanation_en: A bonds price/value has an inverse relationship with interest rates. Since interest rates are increasing (from 8% when issued to 10% now) the bond will be selling at a discount. This happens so an investor will be able to purchase the bond and still earn the same yield that the market currently offers.

explanation_en: As the bond was issued 4 years ago, its remaining maturity is 16 years. The price is calculated as follows: PMT = 6% / 2 × $100 = $3. N = 16 × 2 = 32. I/Y = 5.8% / 2 = 2.9%. FV = $100. CPT PV to obtain $102.07.
